forces: Soprano, alto, mixed chorus and orchestra
intro: The fifth movement of Mahler’s Symphony No. 2 “Resurrection”, marked “Im Tempo des Scherzos — Wild herausfahrend”, opens with an orchestral outburst, and voices enter only after marches, distant brass and birdsong. The chorus first sings very softly, and at its last entry organ, bells and the whole orchestra join it in E♭ major.

sections.label: Intro · Scherzo’s outburst returns, full orchestra
sections.mNote: Full orchestra, then a quiet horn passage.

sections.label: A · Horn calls and wind chorales
sections.mNote: Distant brass, descending triplets and pizzicato strings.

sections.label: B · March, begun by percussion
sections.mNote: Fanfares and running strings in Allegro energico.

sections.label: Link · Recitative in cellos, distant trumpets
sections.mNote: Recitative-like phrases interrupt the marching beat.

sections.label: Link · Distant brass and birdsong
sections.mNote: Flute and piccolo alternate with calls from beyond the orchestra.

sections.label: C · Chorus enters unaccompanied, G♭ major
sections.mNote: Unaccompanied voices begin in G♭ major.

sections.label: D · Alto solo with cor anglais
sections.mNote: Cor anglais and muted strings accompany the solo voice.

sections.label: Dev · Chorus with soprano and alto soloists
sections.mNote: Chorus, then soprano and alto soloists together.

sections.label: C′ · Resurrection chorale, organ and brass
sections.mNote: The first choral tune returns in E♭ major.

sections.label: Coda · Bells and the final E♭
sections.mNote: The orchestra plays the ending after the voices stop.

cues.title: Return of the scherzo’s outcry
cues.text: The orchestral outcry from the scherzo breaks in after the silence that follows Urlicht. The horns then play a phrase that later becomes the resurrection theme. The melody appears here before the chorus sings its words.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 2, Hofmeister full score (1897), movement V, opening; the recalled cry and horn theme are described at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-5-lied-2-auferstehung-im-tempo-des-scherzos/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Offstage horns and wind chorale
cues.text: Horns play calls from offstage. Descending triplets pass down through the winds, and a measured wind chorale moves over pizzicato string quavers. Pauses separate these sections, and each has its own instruments and its own distance.
cues.evidence: The offstage horns, descending triplets and wind chorale over pizzicato quavers belong to the orchestral prelude: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-5-lied-2-auferstehung-im-tempo-des-scherzos/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Wind chorale over pizzicato strings
cues.text: After a silence, flute, oboe and clarinet play a chorale pianissimo over pizzicato violas and cellos. It recalls the Dies irae from the first movement’s funeral march. Some of its intervals anticipate the resurrection theme.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 142 (Langsam, quasi l’istesso Tempo): flute, oboe and clarinet play the chorale pianissimo over pizzicato violas and cellos, with four flats in the signature. The Mahler Foundation’s page on the movement describes a wind chorale against pizzicato quavers that recalls the first movement’s Dies irae and announces intervals of the resurrection theme: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-5-lied-2-auferstehung-im-tempo-des-scherzos/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bülow’s memorial service, Hamburg, 1894
cues.text: At Hans von Bülow’s memorial service in Hamburg on 29 March 1894, Mahler heard Klopstock’s resurrection hymn. He used its first two stanzas for the finale and wrote the rest of the text himself.
cues.evidence: Memorial service and hymn: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-history/ . Klopstock’s first two stanzas and Mahler’s continuation are printed in the full score.

cues.title: Chorale, solo trombone and trumpet
cues.text: A solo trombone, marked bestimmt (decisively), takes up the chorale, and a trumpet follows. The horns then come to the front, the offstage horns play again, and the string tremolo dies away to nothing.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 142, rehearsal 5: first trombone p bestimmt, then first trumpet, over pizzicato strings. P. 143, rehearsal 6 (Nicht eilen): horns marked sehr hervortretend, a group of horns in the distance (stark geblasen), and divided string tremolo marked verhallend, dying away.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Woodwind climax, rehearsal 7 to 8
cues.text: Figures pass between the winds and quicken. Mahler marks Etwas drängend, somewhat pressing, then Sehr drängend, very pressing, and the woodwinds rise to fortissimo. The sound then falls away to the low trombones and a faint timpani roll.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 145 (rehearsal 7, Etwas drängend), p. 146 (rehearsal 8, Sehr drängend, with flutes, oboes, cor anglais, clarinets and bassoons at ff) and p. 147 (Wieder zurückhaltend: low trombones and a timpani roll fading to ppp).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Chorale for low brass, rehearsal 10
cues.text: After a general pause the trombones and tuba, with the contrabassoon, play a broad chorale, Wieder sehr breit. The trumpets join at Etwas energischer, and a long crescendo leads to a brass fanfare.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 148, rehearsal 10: G.P., then Wieder sehr breit for contrabassoon, trombones and tuba with five flats in the signature; Etwas energischer im Tempo brings in the trumpets under a long crescendo, with a conductor’s note on the crescendo. The Mahler Foundation’s page describes a reply in the form of a chorale to which the lower brass add solemnity, followed by the return of the brass fanfare: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-5-lied-2-auferstehung-im-tempo-des-scherzos/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the fanfare in C major
cues.text: The brass fanfare returns in C major. Horns and trumpets exchange repeated calls over harps and cymbals, while the winds and strings play running figures. The resurrection theme is heard again, far more assertive than before.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 149–151: rehearsal 11 (Wieder breit, no sharps or flats in the signature), horn and trumpet volleys with harp glissandos and cymbals on p. 150, woodwind and string runs from rehearsal 12 on p. 151. The Mahler Foundation’s page says the return of the brass fanfare prepares a new statement of the resurrection theme, now far more assertive: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-5-lied-2-auferstehung-im-tempo-des-scherzos/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Percussion crescendo and march
cues.text: A percussion crescendo leads to a brass fanfare and the Allegro energico. Earlier themes return as a march, with sharply articulated rhythms and fast string figures. Mahler marks the passage Nicht zu schnell (not too fast).
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 154–155: percussion crescendo, Maestoso fanfare, Allegro energico, Nicht zu schnell and Sehr scharf rhythmisiert.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dies irae as a march
cues.text: The Dies irae becomes a march, serious and at first upbeat, and the trumpets play a chorale-like variation of the same melody above it. At Kräftig (vigorously), Mahler’s note in the score states that a brisk march tempo has now been reached.
cues.evidence: Bettie Jo Basinger, Utah Symphony listening guide: the Dies irae becomes a serious, initially upbeat march, with a trumpet chorale-like variation of the same melody above it: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide . Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 158: Kräftig, with the note that a fresh march tempo has been reached in the course of the pressing movement (Hier ist im Verlaufe des drängenden Satzes ein frisches Marschtempo erreicht worden).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Low bells during the march
cues.text: Deep bells of no fixed pitch sound against the march, and shortly before they enter the woodwinds raise their bells. Mahler wrote for three such bells, in three passages of the movement totalling twenty-two bars.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 160 (rehearsal 16: Schalltrichter auf in the woodwinds) and p. 161 (Wieder etwas gehaltener; a staff for 3 Stahlstäbe oder Glocken von tiefem und unbestimmtem Klange); further bell staves in the coda, pp. 206–209. The Mahler Foundation’s page lists three low bells in three passages of the movement, 22 bars in total: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-5-lied-2-auferstehung-im-tempo-des-scherzos/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Composition of the finale, 1894
cues.text: Mahler jotted down sketches for the finale as soon as he reached home from Bülow’s funeral, and completed it within about three weeks the following summer. He signed the autograph full score of the whole symphony on 18 December 1894.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation introduction gives the immediate sketches and the three weeks of composition: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-introduction/ . Its history page dates the autograph full score to 18 December 1894: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-history/

cues.title: Cellos and bassoons, distant trumpets
cues.text: The march breaks off into speech-like phrases in the strings. Cellos and bassoons play the melody in the foreground, and distant trumpets and percussion continue behind them. At rehearsal 22 Mahler directed the conductor to keep the far-off fanfares from disturbing the melody.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 174–176, especially rehearsal 22 on p. 175 and its direction about balancing the distant instruments against cellos and bassoons.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: “O glaube” theme, cellos
cues.text: The cellos play the “O glaube” material in phrases that move between duple and triple metres. Much later the alto sings “O glaube, mein Herz” (believe, my heart) to a return of the same phrases.
cues.evidence: Bettie Jo Basinger, Utah Symphony listening guide: the development resumes with the “O glaube” material, and Mahler later sets the text to these pleading phrases: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide . Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 174 (cellos molto espress. after the solo trombone) and p. 175, rehearsal 22 (Mit etwas drängendem Charakter): cellos and first bassoon in changing 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 bars.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Offstage band
cues.text: Far off, a band of trumpets, triangle, cymbals and bass drum plays fanfare signals across the cellos’ line, repeatedly. Mahler sets the band at the greatest distance and at one point asks for it to sound much stronger.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 175 (rehearsal 22) and pp. 176–179 (rehearsals 23–25): trumpets in F and in C, several players each, with triangle, cymbals and bass drum, marked in weitester Ferne aufgestellt; p. 178 carries the direction Hier soll die Musik viel stärker hörbar sein. The Mahler Foundation’s page describes offstage brass superimposing fanfare motifs on the recitative as one of the earliest instances of a spatialization effect: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-5-lied-2-auferstehung-im-tempo-des-scherzos/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Climax, rehearsal 26
cues.text: At rehearsal 26 Mahler marks Più mosso and molto accelerando. Woodwind, horns and trumpets play fortissimo over triangle, bass drum, cymbals, tam-tam and timpani. Mahler’s programme for the passage read: “The earth trembles, the graves burst open, the dead arise and march forth in endless procession.”
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 181–182 (rehearsal 26: Più mosso, molto accelerando, Ganze Takte schlagen, Poco rit.; woodwind, horn and trumpet staves at ff to fff, with triangle, bass drum, cymbals, tam-tam and timpani). Bettie Jo Basinger, Utah Symphony listening guide: the tempo accelerates, the volume rises and the dissonance increases before horn fanfares surface from the din: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide . The programme text, in the Foundation’s translation: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-introduction/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Langsam after the climax, rehearsal 27
cues.text: At rehearsal 27 the climax breaks off, and Mahler marks Langsam, immer noch mehr zurückhaltend. Three pairs of horns play pp chords over a timpani tremolo, sempre pp. The oboe and cellos play separate lines, and the clarinets are marked “(Echo)”.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 183, rehearsal 27: Langsam, immer noch mehr zurückhaltend; five flats in the signature; pp horn chords in three pairs, timpani tremolo sempre pp, glockenspiel, oboe and cello lines, and the clarinets marked (Echo).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Distant brass and birdsong
cues.text: At the great summons the main orchestra drops out for long stretches. Trumpets play from opposing directions and horns hold distant notes. Flute and piccolo play birdsong figures, marked wie eine Vogelstimme, and at times a single instrument sounds alone.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 185–186: spatial directions for trumpets, distant horns, and flute and piccolo marked wie eine Vogelstimme.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First complete performance, Berlin, 1895
cues.text: Mahler conducted the first complete performance of the symphony in Berlin on 13 December 1895. Nine months earlier the city had heard only the first three movements. The audience applauded warmly, and the next morning’s newspapers renewed the attacks.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation introduction describes the enthusiastic response and the bitter notices the next morning: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-introduction/ . Its history page dates the first three movements to 4 March 1895 and the complete première to 13 December 1895: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-history/

cues.title: Mahler’s programme: the nightingale
cues.text: In Mahler’s programme the last trumpet sounds, and the silence that follows holds “a distant nightingale, a last tremulous echo of earthly life”. In the score the flute and piccolo play this passage, marked to sound like a bird’s voice.
cues.evidence: Programme text in the Mahler Foundation introduction: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-introduction/ . Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide links the nightingale to the flute marked wie eine Vogelstimme: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide

cues.title: Entry of the chorus, G♭ major
cues.text: At rehearsal 31, marked Langsam. Misterioso, the chorus enters a cappella in G♭ major at ppp. Klopstock’s hymn promises that dust will rise again after a short rest. The soprano soloist sings within the choral sound, and Mahler marked her part “ohne im Geringsten hervorzutreten”.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 186, rehearsal 31: Langsam. Misterioso, chorus a cappella at ppp, soprano ohne im Geringsten hervorzutreten. The opening text is Klopstock’s.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mahler alters Klopstock
cues.text: Klopstock wrote that the one who made you (“der dich schuf”) will give you immortal life. Mahler sets “der dich rief”: the one who called you. He also turns “I shall be sown” into “you will be sown”, and drops the Hallelujahs.
cues.evidence: Paul Banks’s Mahler catalogue prints Klopstock’s text (Wird, der dich schuf; werd ich gesät; Halleluja) beside Mahler’s version (der dich rief; wirst du gesät): https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/Symph2/Texts.htm

cues.title: Orchestral interlude after first stanza
cues.text: The chorus completes its first stanza, with the soprano soloist singing within its line, and the orchestra continues alone. Mahler marks Sehr breit, very broad, for horns and trumpets in portamento, then Streng im Tempo, strictly in time, with long bows in the strings. The chorus returns for the second stanza.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 187 (rehearsal 32: “Unsterblich Leben wird, der dich rief, dir geben”, with the soprano soloist among the choral staves; rehearsal 33: Sehr breit, horns and trumpets molto portamento) and pp. 188–189 (rehearsal 34: Streng im Tempo, first and second violins lang gezogen, viel Bogen). Bettie Jo Basinger, Utah Symphony listening guide: an orchestral interlude follows the first stanza, and the chorus interrupts it to deliver the second: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Klopstock’s second stanza
cues.text: Klopstock’s second stanza reads “To bloom again you are sown! The Lord of the harvest goes and gathers in, like sheaves, us who died.” The chorus sings it quietly. An orchestral interlude then ends Klopstock’s text, and Mahler’s own words follow.
cues.evidence: Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide prints Klopstock’s stanzas and Mahler’s continuation in German and English, and describes the second stanza and the orchestral interlude that ends Klopstock’s text: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide . Translation by the site.

cues.title: DuPage Symphony Orchestra, Wheaton, 2004
cues.text: This is Barbara Schubert’s DuPage Symphony Orchestra in Edman Memorial Chapel, Wheaton College, Illinois, on 22 May 2004. Eric Pancer taped the concert on a Sony MiniDisc recorder. He put it on the Internet Archive that December.
cues.evidence: Internet Archive item metadata for “Resurrection!” (taper, equipment, venue, concert date and upload dates): https://archive.org/details/dupageso-2004-05-22

cues.title: Alto solo, B♭ minor
cues.text: Mahler’s own words begin with an appeal to the heart. The alto sings in B♭ minor beside a cor anglais, over muted strings and plucked bass notes.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 193, rehearsal 39: O glaube, mein Herz, o glaube, alto with cor anglais, muted divided strings and pizzicato basses.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Soprano solo, rehearsal 41
cues.text: The soprano follows the alto: “O believe, you were not born in vain!” A solo violin on the D string continues her line over tremolo strings. At rehearsal 42 a harp glissando, its first note strongly accented, leads upward into the next section.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 194 (rehearsal 41: soprano solo “O glaube: Du wardst nicht umsonst geboren!”) and p. 195 (soprano continuing; first violin Solo on the D string; harp glissando at rehearsal 42 with the instruction that its first note be strongly accented). The soprano’s line follows the alto’s in Mahler’s text, printed in German in Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide . Translation by the site.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Rehearsal 42, Mahler’s own text
cues.text: Low voices bring back the resurrection theme with Mahler’s own words, “Was entstanden ist, das muss vergehen”, over trombones, tuba and a high violin trill. The chorus sings “auferstehen”. Alto and chorus then sing “Hör’ auf zu beben!” (stop trembling) at ppp, followed by “Bereite dich zu leben!” (prepare to live).
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 195 (rehearsal 42, Langsamer. Misterioso: alto, tenor and bass sing “Was entstanden ist, das muss vergehen”, with trombones and tuba and violin trills), p. 196 (rehearsal 43: “auferstehen”, then “Hör’ auf zu beben” at ppp with the alto soloist marked ohne hervorzutreten, then “Bereite dich zu leben”, Schneller) and p. 197. Bettie Jo Basinger, Utah Symphony listening guide: the chorus returns with the Auferstehen material, now singing Mahler’s text: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Duet for alto and soprano
cues.text: Alto and soprano sing “O Schmerz! Du Alldurchdringer!” (O pain, all-penetrating one). Mahler marks the passage Mit Aufschwung, aber nicht eilen (with uplift, but not hurrying), and later Vorwärts and Drängend. The duet briefly refers to the melody of Urlicht.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 197 (rehearsal 44: Mit Aufschwung, aber nicht eilen; “O Schmerz! Du Alldurchdringer!”), p. 198 (rehearsal 45: “O Tod! Du Allbezwinger!”) and p. 199 (Vorwärts, Drängend, Nicht schleppen: “Mit Flügeln … werd’ ich entschweben”). Bettie Jo Basinger, Utah Symphony listening guide: the passage marked Mit Aufschwung, and the duet’s reference to the Urlicht melody: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the choral melody
cues.text: The first choral melody, first heard without accompaniment, returns in E♭ major with brass and organ. Soprano and alto join the chorus. The organ is marked volles Werk, full organ.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 204, rehearsal 48: Aufersteh’n return, soloists with chorus, brass and organ marked volles Werk.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mahler on the final climax
cues.text: Mahler told Natalie Bauer-Lechner that the build-up and surge of the closing pages were “so immense that afterwards even I do not know how I came to write it”.
cues.evidence: Natalie Bauer-Lechner, Erinnerungen an Gustav Mahler (Leipzig: E. P. Tal, 1923), pp. 23–24, in the section “Deutung der Zweiten Symphonie”: “Die Steigerung und der Aufschwung, der jetzt bis zum Schlusse folgt, ist ein so ungeheurer, daß ich selbst hinterher nicht weiß, wie ich dazu gelangen konnte.” Translation ours. https://archive.org/details/erinnerungengust00baue . The Mahler Foundation’s page on the Collier bell foundry quotes the same remark in English: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/locations/germany/berlin/city-of-berlin//bell-foundry-collier/

cues.title: Letter to Anna von Mildenburg, 1895
cues.text: On 8 December 1895, five days before the première, Mahler wrote to the soprano Anna von Mildenburg about the bells he needed. He had taken the train through snow-covered fir woods to a foundry at Zehlendorf, because “only a bell founder could help me”.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation quotes Mahler’s letter of 8 December 1895 to Anna Bahr-von Mildenburg about his visit to the Collier foundry: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/locations/germany/berlin/city-of-berlin//bell-foundry-collier/

cues.title: Orchestral close in E♭ major
cues.text: After the singers finish, the orchestra continues with organ and bells in E♭ major. On the last page Mahler marks Mit höchster Kraftentfaltung (with the utmost force), then a sharply cut-off ending, scharf abgerissen. The whole orchestra releases the final chord together.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 206–209; p. 209 gives Mit höchster Kraftentfaltung and scharf abgerissen.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Trumpets over the closing chord
cues.text: Over a sustained E♭ major chord the trumpets play a short two-note figure again and again, loud and then louder. All ten horns play the long closing chord with the full orchestra, organ and bells.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 208–209: horn staves for players 1 to 10, trumpets repeating a two-note figure marked ff and then fff over Noch einmal so langsam, organ volles Werk, a bell staff and tam-tam, and scharf abreissen on the last bar. Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide gives the movement ten horns, four of them offstage earlier: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Horn calls emerge from the outburst
transitions.from: Intro · Scherzo’s outburst returns, full orchestra
transitions.to: A · Horn calls and wind chorales
transitions.how: The opening orchestral outburst dies away into horn phrases separated by pauses. Offstage horns enter in reply, and descending triplets pass down through the winds. The prelude then sets a wind chorale over pizzicato quavers in the strings.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 134–145; prelude described at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-5-lied-2-auferstehung-im-tempo-des-scherzos/

transitions.title: Percussion leads into the brass fanfare
transitions.from: A · Horn calls and wind chorales
transitions.how: The percussion enters as the prelude dies away and leads into a Maestoso brass fanfare. In the Allegro energico that follows, the strings play running figures beneath sharply accented march figures. Mahler marks the passage Nicht zu schnell, which keeps the beat firm under the quick notes.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister full score (1897), movement V, pp. 154–155.

transitions.title: Cello recitative after the march
transitions.to: Link · Recitative in cellos, distant trumpets
transitions.how: The march breaks off, and the cellos play irregular phrases in the manner of a recitative. Bassoons join them above restrained strings. Distant trumpet and percussion calls continue separately. At rehearsal 22 the score gives an explicit balance instruction that the trumpet and percussion calls must not cover the cello and bassoon melody.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 174–176, rehearsal 22 and its balance instruction.

transitions.title: Distant brass and birdsong
transitions.from: Link · Recitative in cellos, distant trumpets
transitions.how: The strings stop. Horns and trumpets play calls separated by long held notes and pauses, and the score directs the trumpets to sound from opposite sides. Between the brass notes, flute and piccolo play short, quick birdsong figures from nearby.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 183–186, especially the spatial directions on p. 185.

transitions.title: Unaccompanied chorus in G♭ major
transitions.to: C · Chorus enters unaccompanied, G♭ major
transitions.how: The distant calls and the birdsong stop. At Langsam. Misterioso the chorus enters in G♭ major, a cappella and ppp. The soprano soloist sings within the upper choral line, and the basses take the lowest part, which the orchestra no longer plays.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 186, rehearsal 31.

transitions.title: Alto and cor anglais in B♭ minor
transitions.from: C · Chorus enters unaccompanied, G♭ major
transitions.to: D · Alto solo with cor anglais
transitions.how: After the choral stanzas and the orchestral replies between them, the alto enters in B♭ minor. A cor anglais plays a line around the vocal part, accompanied by muted divided strings and pizzicato basses. The soprano then takes up the appeal.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 193–194, rehearsal 39 onwards.

transitions.title: From the soprano’s phrase to the chorus
transitions.from: D · Alto solo with cor anglais
transitions.to: Dev · Chorus with soprano and alto soloists
transitions.how: The soprano’s phrase slows and the strings drop back. A harp glissando leads to the entry of the lower choral voices, and trumpets, trombones and tuba follow their measured phrases. Mahler marks the passage Langsamer. Misterioso. The soloists’ duet then begins and rises.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 195, rehearsal 42, and the subsequent duet.

transitions.title: Organ joins the E♭ major chorus
transitions.from: Dev · Chorus with soprano and alto soloists
transitions.to: C′ · Resurrection chorale, organ and brass
transitions.how: Overlapping choral lines rise through a crescendo. The resurrection melody returns in E♭ major, marked Pesante, and the soloists join the chorus. At rehearsal 48 the full organ enters, marked volles Werk. With broad brass chords, it holds the harmony beneath the voices through their long phrases.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 202–204, reaching rehearsal 48 with organ marked volles Werk.

transitions.title: Choral close to orchestral final page
transitions.from: C′ · Resurrection chorale, organ and brass
transitions.to: Coda · Bells and the final E♭
transitions.how: The voices finish and the instruments continue in E♭ major. Brass, strings and organ hold the closing harmony, and bells sound above the bass. On the final page the tempo slows to half speed, marked Noch einmal so langsam, and the orchestra cuts off the last chord together, marked scharf abgerissen.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 206–209; Noch einmal so langsam and scharf abgerissen on the final page.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 2, full score (Hofmeister 1897; Weinberger/Universal Edition reprint)
source.locator: Finale, pp. 134–209: orchestral prelude and march, distant calls, a cappella chorus, soprano and alto solos, and the E♭-major ending with organ and bells.

timeline.note: Brass and strings play the opening outburst; the voices and organ do not play.
Separate horn calls and wind phrases follow the opening outburst.
Wind chorales and descending figures alternate above moving and plucked strings.
A percussion crescendo leads into brass fanfares and a march with running strings.
Cellos and bassoons play against distant trumpets and percussion; the other strings hold back.
Distant horns, trumpets and percussion answer the nearby flute and piccolo birdsong.
The chorus begins without accompaniment; the soprano soloist blends into its sound.
Winds, brass and strings answer the chorus’s first stanza.
The voices begin the second Klopstock stanza quietly, and the strings enter around their phrases.
The alto sings with the cor anglais over muted strings; the soprano then takes up the appeal.
Soprano and alto sing of pain and death, with strings, harp and soft wind and brass phrases.
Chorus and soloists sing the resurrection theme with brass, strings and full organ.
Organ, bells and orchestra complete the E♭-major ending after the voices finish.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor.
